1. The project at a glance

EdaphNet is a research project, with working software, that asks whether a cheap, independent observation of a soil sample (mainly its colour, as a phone camera could record it, or a laboratory spectrum) can tell a soil-testing laboratory which reports to re-test and what went wrong with them. It checks a whole laboratory batch at once for two kinds of mistakes: a report that belongs to another sample (a swap) and a single corrupted number (a value error). This dossier is the complete record of the project: what it is for, how it was built, what data and models it uses, what was tested and measured, what is new, what failed, and what happens next.

2. Problem statement and motivation

2.1 Soil reports drive real decisions

A soil test report decides how much fertiliser and lime a farmer applies and, increasingly, how much carbon a field is credited with. Public programmes test soils at very large scale. Laboratories control quality with reference samples, proficiency testing and plausibility rules, but these work at the level of the laboratory. The individual farmer who receives one report has no independent way to know whether that report is right for their sample. Measurement disagreement is not rare: in one comparison of eight service laboratories, 28% of soil organic carbon results fell outside the acceptable range of the North American Proficiency Testing programme (cited in the paper draft; to be verified against the full text).

2.2 Failure 1: swapped samples are invisible to every lab-only check

Samples are mislabelled, placed in the wrong tray position, or a whole tray is shifted by one place. The farmer then receives the results of another soil. A swapped report looks perfectly normal, because it is a real report of a different soil: every value is plausible, every internal rule is satisfied. Only something that observes the physical sample itself can reveal the mismatch.

2.3 Failure 2: corrupted values

Single numbers are corrupted by decimal slips (×10, ÷10), unit confusion, transposed digits (0.16 → 0.61), interchanged columns, or analytical failures (gross errors). Some of these are caught by range checks; many are not, because the wrong value can still be plausible.

2.4 Failure 3: re-testing everything is unaffordable

Re-analysing every sample doubles the cost of testing. A laboratory can afford to re-test only a small share of reports, so it needs a ranked list: which few reports are most likely wrong, and what to look for when re-testing them.

2.5 Why this is a research problem and not only an engineering one

A cheap witness such as soil colour is weak: it explains carbon well but most other properties poorly. Whether such a weak signal is enough to find errors, which errors it can find, how it should be combined across a batch where swaps involve several reports at once, and whether false alarms can be controlled with realistic calibration data are open questions. The answers are not obvious in advance, and the project shows that some intuitive answers are wrong (for example, that the joint model's advantage would be largest for the weakest witness).

3. Research objectives and questions

3.1 Aim

To design, build and evaluate, with rules fixed in advance, a method that uses an independent observation of each soil sample to rank the reports of a laboratory batch for re-testing, explain what went wrong, and propose a correction, and to establish when such a cheap witness is enough.

3.3 Research questions

  • RQ1. Can an independent observation of the sample make report errors detectable that lab-only checks miss, and which ones?
  • RQ2. Does a joint batch model over swaps and value errors find more errors than the best existing method within a fixed re-test budget, and for which witness strength?
  • RQ3. Can the model say correctly what went wrong (swap partner, error type)?
  • RQ4. Can false alarms be controlled at a stated rate with realistic calibration data, and what does that require?
  • RQ5. How does the answer to RQ2 depend on the mix of swaps and value errors, and on error types the model does not know?

4. Scope and boundaries

4.1 In scope

  • Errors: sample swaps (neighbour swaps, tray shifts, random pairs) and single-value errors (×10, ÷10, unit confusion, digit transposition, column interchange, gross analytical error); in a separate test, four error types the model does not know.
  • Witnesses: none (W0); soil colour in CIELAB with phone-like noise ΔE 0, 2, 4, 8 (W1); 10 visible bands (W2); the full Vis-NIR spectrum (W3).
  • Data: open soil spectral libraries with real laboratory values (KSSL: organic carbon, nitrogen, total carbon; ICRAF-ISRIC: eight properties).
  • Output: a suspicion score, an explanation and a proposed correction for every report; a re-test list at a fixed budget; optionally flags with a target false-alarm rate.

4.2 Deliberately out of scope in this study

4.3 What the project explicitly does not claim

It does not claim that a phone photo can replace a laboratory test, that colour alone beats existing checks, that the method has been validated on real photographs or real laboratory errors, or that any number applies to Indian soils. Every result is labelled as pre-registered or exploratory.

A recent open dataset evaluates smartphone imaging for soil organic carbon across four phones on 84 samples (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.22876123, 2026). It predicts properties; it does not check reports. No soil laboratory-error benchmark was found (LimeSoDa and REIN are the nearest; neither contains laboratory errors).

5.3 What the field looks like as a whole

Three traditions exist and do not meet. Proximal soil sensing (smartphone colour, spectroscopy) predicts properties but never asks whether a laboratory report is right. Laboratory and clinical quality control checks values against predictions or history, and genomics detects sample swaps, but with near-perfect witnesses or with patient history rather than an independent look at the same specimen. Statistical error detection (cleanlab, conformal outlier testing) provides general tools without the structure of laboratory errors (trays, typed slips). EdaphNet sits where the three meet: a weak, independent observation of the specimen, used jointly across a batch, with typed errors and a stated false-alarm rate.

Statement of what is not claimed. Flagging values via predictions, conformal p-values with Benjamini–Hochberg, cross-modal swap matching, unit-error tables and phone soil colour are existing tools used as components. The method does not beat the best existing method with a colour witness at an equal mix of errors (pre-registered A1 failed). The structured swap prior gave no benefit (H6 not supported). The exploratory results (error mix, per-batch control, gross-error diagnosis) are hypotheses for confirmation, not proven claims. A reviewer may call C1 "Broman + Bates + a unit table"; the defence is C2 and C3, which no component alone provides.

8.2 Experiment flow

One experiment setting runs as follows: the runner loads the dataset and witness predictions for the chosen witness rung → splits test samples into batches of 24 in random or clustered order → plants swaps and value errors with a seeded random generator → scores every batch with EdaphNet, its four ablations and the seven baselines → computes conformal p-values from clean calibration reports → measures recall at a 5% budget and power/FDR at q = 0.10 per pool of 50 batches → writes all scores and metrics to the run folder → moves to the next setting. Seeds are derived from (seed, rung, ordering) with a stable hash, so an interrupted run resumes with identical numbers.

9.5 What the data look like

KSSL covers a wide range of organic carbon, from mineral subsoils (≈ 0.1%) to organic horizons (> 30%), which is why colour, which mostly tracks darkness and therefore carbon, explains KSSL carbon well. ICRAF-ISRIC is smaller but covers more properties that colour does not see (pH, CEC, potassium, texture).

10. Methodology

10.1 Witness model

Each property x is mapped to a standardised latent scale z (identity, log or logit, per property). Given the witness w of a sample (its CIELAB colour, 10 visible bands, or 30 principal components of the spectrum), the predicted latent properties are

p(z | w) = Normal( μ(w), Σ )

where μ(w) is a gradient-boosted regression per property and Σ is the full covariance of out-of-fold residuals. Because Σ is full, the model knows how carbon, nitrogen and total carbon move together, so one corrupted value can show up as an inconsistency with the others even where the witness says little about that property.

10.2 Value-error library

Table 15. The value-error library 𝒞 (at most one corrupted value per report; equal prior per group, uniform within a group).

Error groupOperation on the printed valueExample
Decimal slip× 10 or ÷ 10OC 0.82 → 8.2
Unit confusionConversion between units used for that property (e.g. % vs g/kg)OC 1.2 % printed as 12 (g/kg)
Digit transpositionTwo adjacent digits of the printed number exchanged0.16 → 0.61
Column interchangeValues of two properties exchangedN and OC columns swapped
Gross analytical errorMultiplicative factor on a grid in [1/3, 0.8] ∪ [1.25, 3]OC measured 2× too high

10.3 Swap hypotheses

The enumerated set: identity (no swap); adjacent transpositions; cyclic rotations by ±1 (blocks of length ≥ 3) and ±2 (length ≥ 5), which model a tray shifted by one or two places; and arbitrary pair transpositions. A structured prior gives tray-like patterns more weight; a uniform prior is tested as an ablation.

10.4 Joint batch inference

For report j and candidate sample i, the evidence that report j was measured on sample i, allowing any corruption c, is

ℓ(j, i) = log Σc P(c) · p( Tc−1(rj) | wi ) · |Jc|

where Tc is the corruption, rj the printed report and |Jc| the Jacobian of the transformation. The log-posterior of a swap hypothesis π is

log P(π) + Σj moved by π [ ℓ(j, π(j)) − ℓ(j, j) ]

normalised over the enumerated set, so inference is exact over that set. For each report: P(clean) = (1 − P(moved)) · P(c = none | rj, wj); the suspicion score is 1 − P(clean); the explanation is the most likely swap partner or the most likely corruption; the correction is the inverse of that corruption.

10.5 Re-test policy

Reports are ranked by suspicion within a pool of 50 batches (about one laboratory day), and the top 5% are re-tested (the primary metric of amendment v2). Ties are broken at random with a fixed seed.

10.6 False-alarm control

For a stated false-discovery rate, each test report gets a conformal p-value against N clean calibration reports, p = (1 + #{calibration scores ≥ s}) / (N + 1), and Benjamini–Hochberg is applied at q = 0.10 per pool. Each distinct calibration sample contributes one score (Section 14.4). Weighted and per-group (Mondrian) calibration were also tested for shift between batches.

10.7 Error injection protocol

In each test batch of 24: with probability 0.2 a swap event (adjacent swap, tray shift or pair swap, equally likely); every other report receives a value error with probability 0.025, drawn from the library (or, in the unknown-error test, from four types outside it: ×100, gross ×4–8, a value copied from the neighbouring report, a dropped digit). About 5% of reports are erroneous, roughly half of them swaps. Batches are formed either in random order or clustered (layers of the same profile or location together), the harder case.

Nine experiments were run. Every one writes a run folder with its configuration, code version and environment, and every number below can be regenerated with the commands in Section 19. Experiments X1–X5 were planned in the specification; X5 was the pre-registered test. X6–X9 are exploratory and are labelled as such wherever they are reported.

On planted errors. With real laboratory reports nobody knows which ones are wrong, so detection rates cannot be measured. Planting errors in real reports is the standard way to obtain ground truth. It is a genuine limitation for external validity (the real mix and the real types are unknown), and it is why X7 (unknown types) and X9 (other mixes) were run, and why paper 2 uses blind duplicates.

13. Evaluation metrics

13.1 Detection and control metrics

Table 21. Metrics and their interpretation.

MetricDefinitionWhy it matters
Recall at 5% budget (primary)Share of erroneous reports inside the top 5% most suspicious reports of each pool of 50 batchesWhat a laboratory gets when it can afford to re-test 5%
Power at FDR q = 0.10Share of erroneous reports flagged by Benjamini–Hochberg at q = 0.10Detection when false alarms must be controlled
Realised FDRShare of flagged reports that were actually cleanWhether the stated false-alarm rate holds
Attribution accuracyShare of flagged value errors whose type is named correctly; share of flagged swaps whose partner is correctWhether the laboratory learns what to look for
Recall by error typeRecall at budget per error type and witness rungThe detectability map
R² (witness)Share of a property's variation explained by the witness on unseen locationsHow informative the witness is
AUPRCArea under the precision–recall curveRanking quality independent of a threshold

13.2 Statistical protocol

  • Paired comparisons: all methods are scored on identical batches with identical planted errors.
  • Intervals: 95% cluster-bootstrap intervals over pools (2,000 resamples), because reports in one pool are not independent.
  • Pre-registration: pass/fail rules and the verdict script were committed before the data they judge (docs 11, 18).
  • Seeds: fixed per (seed, witness, ordering) with a stable hash; resumed runs give identical numbers (tested).

13.3 Metrics not used, and why

  • Real error rates and laboratory cost savings: need real errors (paper 2).
  • Accuracy on real phone photos: needs paired photos and reports (paper 2).
  • Overall accuracy: misleading at 5% prevalence; a checker that flags nothing is 95% accurate.

14. Results

14.1 X2 — what a witness knows about real soils

Colour computed from laboratory spectra explains organic carbon well on KSSL (R² 0.72; 0.70 with phone-like noise ΔE 2), nitrogen and total carbon moderately (0.55, 0.69), and on ICRAF-ISRIC organic carbon only moderately (0.37) and little else (pH 0.27, Ca 0.23, clay 0.16, CEC 0.11, K 0.07, sand 0.02). A spectrometer explains 0.39–0.90 of all properties. Colour mainly knows carbon.

14.2 X1 — simulation: the mechanism works with a moderately informative witness

With no or very weak witness (λ ≤ 0.5) EdaphNet and the best baseline are equal. From λ = 1 the gap opens, and it peaks at λ = 2 (random batches: 0.65 vs 0.42 of errors caught at FDR 0.10), where colour explains about 66% of carbon. At λ = 4 the baselines catch up partly. The gain came almost entirely from swaps; the swap partner was correct in 87–91% of flagged swaps at λ = 2. The prediction that the gain would be largest for the weakest witness (H2) was refuted.

14.3 X3 — first real test (ICRAF-ISRIC): failed, with a flawed calibration

The original primary test (power at FDR 0.10 with a phone-grade colour witness) did not pass: +0.03 and +0.05 in random batches, −0.05 and −0.01 in clustered batches. The realised FDR of most baselines was 0.4–0.9, far above the target. The diagnosis (14.4) showed that this was mainly caused by our calibration design, so the comparison was not valid in either direction. The verdict is reported as recorded.

14.4 X4 — calibration diagnostic: reused calibration samples break false-alarm control

The step-5 runner reused about 511 calibration samples across 400 calibration batches, so the same sample contributed many scores. Conformal p-values assume exchangeable, distinct calibration scores; counting one sample many times makes them too small and inflates false alarms. On the calibration split only (no test data touched), keeping one score per distinct sample brought the realised FDR of range checks from 0.57 to 0.00 and of the lab-only model from 0.63 to 0.07 in the reported setting, and to or below the target on average (Figure 6). With only ~260 distinct calibration samples, however, power fell to about zero. This was our design error; it is recorded in decisions D-016 and D-017 and in a correction note to doc 17.

The swap hypotheses and the witness create the swap advantage (+0.39 to +0.56). The value-error library is a trade-off: it helps value errors slightly and costs swaps more with colour. The structured swap prior has no effect (H6 not supported, again).

14.8 Detectability by error type

Swaps are almost invisible without a witness (0.05) and become findable with colour (0.34–0.46) and much more with a spectrometer (0.75). Column interchanges and decimal slips are found well by every method. Digit transpositions (≈ 0.1) and gross errors stay hard; gross errors favour B5 strongly (14.9).

14.9 X8 — gross errors: a limitation, not a bug (exploratory)

An external review noted that several EdaphNet variants gave exactly the same gross-error recall (0.034). The diagnosis found no scoring artefact: 0.034 = 7 of 208 errors, a small-count coincidence, and no budget cut fell inside a tie of zero scores. EdaphNet ranks gross errors above most reports (median 75th percentile) but rarely in the top 5%, and explains 178 of the 201 it misses as a digit transposition or a column interchange. The baselines that catch them use the hard constraint that organic carbon cannot exceed total carbon (B1 explicitly, B5 by learning it); gross errors on nitrogen, which break no such constraint, are hard for all. The Gaussian witness model captures the correlation between carbon properties but not this inequality; adding hard constraints is a direct extension.

With colour, EdaphNet beats the best baseline once 60–70% of errors are swaps; with a spectrometer, from 30%. It beats the swap-only matcher B4 at every mix (colour +0.06 to +0.13; spectrometer +0.10 to +0.13). The registered mix (52–56% swaps) sits exactly at the colour crossover, which explains the A1 result. A laboratory that knows its own error mix can read off which checker to use.

14.11 False-alarm control and pool size (exploratory)

On KSSL (~2,800 distinct calibration samples) the false-alarm rate was controlled, but with colour EdaphNet had almost no power at the registered pool of 50 batches. The reason is partly mechanical: a conformal p-value cannot be smaller than 1/(N + 1), and Benjamini–Hochberg over m reports at level q can reject only when at least m / (q(N + 1)) reports reach that floor: about 5 reports for a pool of 1,200, fewer than one for a single batch of 24. Testing one batch at a time restored EdaphNet's power to 0.19–0.25 at realised FDR ≈ 0.10. With colour, B5 kept more power at every pool size (e.g. 0.25 vs 0.19 per batch), though its realised FDR rose to 0.16–0.17 in some clustered settings; with a spectrometer, EdaphNet had more power at every pool size except the largest.

14.12 X7 — errors the model does not know (exploratory, 5 seeds)

The pattern holds: with colour (random batches) swaps +0.103 [0.069, 0.137], wrong values −0.057 [−0.078, −0.036], overall +0.027 [0.009, 0.047]; with a spectrometer swaps +0.147 and wrong values −0.032. Large unknown errors are found by all methods (×100: 0.99 vs 0.91); subtle ones are hard for all (dropped digit 0.14 vs 0.16; neighbour copy 0.42 vs 0.49); gross ×4–8 errors again favour B5 (0.40 vs 0.61). B5 was trained on the same unknown mix, which favours it. Seed 11 reproduced the earlier single-seed run exactly.

14.13 Explaining errors: the clearest advantage

Table 27. Attribution accuracy among flagged errors.

SettingEdaphNetRule-based repair (B6)
KSSL, spectrometer (pre-registered A3)97–100%24–29%
ICRAF-ISRIC89–98%37–51%
Simulation84–92%32–50%

Among the baselines, only rule-based repair states what went wrong with a value; the swap matcher implies a reassignment but cannot explain value errors; B5 and cleanlab only score reports. This is the main practical reason for a joint model: a laboratory re-testing a report also learns what to look for. With colour, fewer than the pre-registered minimum of 30 value errors were flagged per cell, so attribution could not be evaluated there.

14.16 Demonstrators

The live demo (scripts/serve_demo.py) runs the real model on the laptop; its Guided demo plays three cases (a correct report, a ×10 slip, a swapped report) with captions. 15. Limitations and threats to validity

15.1 The four that matter most

Table 30. Principal limitations.

LimitationConsequenceWhat would remove it
Errors were planted, not observed. The real mix of swaps and value errors, and the real error types, are unknown.The overall verdict with colour depends on an assumed mix (Section 14.10).Blind duplicates with a partner laboratory, or laboratory re-test records (paper 2).
No real phone photos. Colour was calculated from laboratory spectra of dried, sieved soil.A best case: real photos (moist soil, shadows, different phones) will be noisier, although they also carry texture.A real-photo study: the Zenodo 84-sample smartphone set, or 30–50 Indian samples with laboratory values.
One main dataset, carbon-only properties. KSSL (USA) measures OC, N and total C, which colour sees best.Results may not transfer to properties colour does not see (pH, P, K) or to other regions.LUCAS confirmation; Indian soils; the ICRAF analysis already shows colour sees little beyond carbon.
Several results are exploratory. Error mix, per-batch control, gross-error diagnosis, unknown types.They explain the verdict but are not proof.Amendment v3 implemented and evaluated on KSSL data; hypothesis C3 confirmed.

15.2 Threats to validity

  • Internal. B5 was trained on the true planted error mix, an advantage it would not have in practice, so comparisons with B5 are conservative for EdaphNet. The error-mix analysis re-ranks stored scores rather than recomputing them, an approximation.
  • External. Planted errors follow the author's model of laboratory mistakes; real laboratories may make other mistakes, at other rates. Clustered batches built from layers of one profile are harsher than typical trays.
  • Construct. Recall at a 5% budget assumes a laboratory re-tests a fixed share; real policies may differ. Calculated colour is a proxy for a phone photograph.
  • Statistical. Intervals are cluster-bootstrap intervals over 30 pools per setting; differences smaller than about ±0.02 are not meaningful.

15.3 Known engineering compromises

  • CPU-only laptop with 7.8 GB RAM: runs are chunked and memory-lean; the main test took about 15 hours of wall-clock time.
  • Run records written before 3 October 2026 carry a wrong label in metrics.json ("ICRAF-ISRIC" for KSSL runs); the correct dataset is in each config.json. The script is fixed; old records are left unchanged.
  • Raw data and per-report predictions are not on GitHub (size); they are rebuildable (Section 19).

16. Research integrity, ethics and licensing

16.1 Integrity rules followed

  • No invented or exaggerated results; every number traceable to a run record.
  • Pass/fail rules and analysis scripts committed before the data they judge (docs 11, 18; commits are dated).
  • Failures reported, not hidden: v1 and v2 main claims failed and are stated as such.
  • Exploratory analyses labelled and written to a separate folder; the method was frozen before the pre-registered test.
  • Mistakes recorded and corrected openly (Table 31).

16.3 Ethics

The study uses public, de-identified soil data only; no human participants and no personal data. The planned paper-2 study (Indian soil samples and photos) involves no personal data beyond field identifiers; farmer names and exact field locations will not be collected. Laboratory partners will be credited as agreed.

17. Intellectual-property position

17.1 What has been prepared

An invention log is kept privately on the laptop (never on GitHub). No invention disclosure has been filed yet. The patent question was deliberately deferred while the research was done.

17.2 Aspects for which protection could be sought

  • Principal: a method that verifies a batch of soil laboratory reports by scoring every report jointly under structured swap hypotheses and a library of typed value errors, using a model of what an independent observation of each physical sample implies, and returns for each report a suspicion score, the most likely error and a correction.
  • Second: the batch-level re-test policy that allocates a fixed re-test budget using these scores, with per-batch false-alarm control.

17.3 Honest assessment of the obstacles

Table 33. Obstacles to a granted patent.

ObstacleWhy it appliesPossible response
India, Section 3(k): computer programme per se, algorithmsA statistical checking method implemented in software is the shape of claim examiners reject.Tie the claim to the physical measurement chain (sample → witness device → laboratory instrument → re-test); weak for a colour witness.
Inventive stepCombining known swap matching (genomics), conformal testing and unit tables may be argued obvious.Show an effect no component gives alone: attribution 97–100% vs 24–29%; the error-mix crossover.
Weak evidence for the core claimWith colour, the main pre-registered claim failed.Any claim would rest on the spectrometer setting or on attribution, not on phone colour.
Public disclosureThe repository was public on GitHub for a period before being made private; India has no general grace period.Report the exact public dates (GitHub history) to the institutional IPR cell before any preprint or further disclosure.

Position. A patent looks unlikely to be strong: the core detection claim with colour failed, software methods face Section 3(k), and the repository was public for a time. Publishing the work openly (paper plus a Zenodo release of the code) is the more realistic route. The decision belongs to the student, the guide and the IPR cell.

20. Conclusion

EdaphNet asked whether a cheap, independent look at a soil sample can tell a laboratory which reports to re-test and what went wrong. The answer, from a pre-registered test on nearly 20,000 real soils, is precise rather than simple. An independent observation makes sample swaps detectable, which no lab-only check can do; with a spectrometer the batch model finds more errors overall than the best existing method (+0.09) and explains them correctly almost every time (97–100%). With colour alone it finds more swaps but fewer wrong values, and at an equal mix it does not win; it pays off when most errors are swaps. Reliable automatic alarms need distinct calibration data in proportion to how many reports are tested at once, and silently fail when calibration samples are reused.

What the project does not have yet is the evidence that matters most in practice: real phone photographs, real laboratory errors, and Indian soils. Those are not caveats added at the end; they are the next study, and its protocol is written. The engineering and the first study are finished, the results are reproducible and stated precisely enough to be attacked, and the next result worth having involves a real laboratory and real samples.

Appendix B. Glossary

Table 39. Terms used in this dossier.

TermMeaning
WitnessA cheap, independent observation of the same physical soil sample (its colour or spectrum) that laboratory data handling cannot corrupt.
SwapA report that belongs to a different sample (mislabelling, wrong tray position, shifted tray).
Value errorOne corrupted number in a report: decimal slip, unit confusion, digit transposition, column interchange, gross error.
Batch / poolA batch is 24 reports (one laboratory tray); a pool is 50 batches (about one laboratory day).
Re-test budgetThe share of reports a laboratory can afford to re-analyse; here the top 5% most suspicious.
Recall at budgetShare of erroneous reports inside the re-test budget.
FDRFalse-discovery rate: the share of flagged reports that were actually correct.
Conformal p-valueHow unusual a report's score is compared with clean calibration reports; smallest possible value 1/(N + 1).
Benjamini–Hochberg (BH)A procedure that flags reports while controlling the FDR at a chosen level q.
Pseudo-replicationCounting the same calibration sample many times as if it were independent; the cause of our early false-alarm failure.
Pre-registrationWriting down and committing the pass/fail rules before running the test that they judge.
ExploratoryAn analysis chosen after seeing results; useful for explanation and new hypotheses, not proof.
AblationRemoving one part of the method to measure what it contributes.
CIELAB, ΔEA standard colour space; ΔE is the size of a colour difference (≈ 2 is a good phone's error).
Vis-NIR spectrumReflectance of the soil across visible and near-infrared light, measured by a laboratory instrument.
Run record / provenanceThe saved record of one experiment: settings, code version, environment, results.
Cluster bootstrapResampling whole pools to get honest intervals when reports within a pool are not independent.
